title: Guru Nanak and the origins of Sikhism
summary: In the Punjab, Guru Nanak preached devotion to one formless God and the equality of all people, founding the Sikh faith.
description: According to Sikh tradition, Nanak, born in 1469 at Talwandi near Lahore, had a revelatory experience around 1499 while bathing in the Bein river at Sultanpur Lodhi and declared that there is no Hindu and no Muslim. He travelled widely and later settled at Kartarpur on the Ravi, where he founded a community bound by shared worship, honest labour and the communal kitchen (langar). His hymns form a core of the Guru Granth Sahib, and he was followed by nine human Gurus. Sikhism today has some 25–30 million adherents, most of them in the Punjab.

title: The Columbian exchange
summary: After 1492 crops, livestock, people and germs crossed the Atlantic: maize and potatoes spread worldwide while horses, wheat and smallpox reached the Americas.
description: The term, coined by the historian Alfred Crosby in 1972, describes the transfer of plants, animals, microbes and people between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that followed Columbus's voyages. American crops such as maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes and chilli peppers became staples from Ireland to China and West Africa, contributing to population growth in the Old World, while tobacco became a worldwide habit and trade good. Horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat, sugarcane and coffee transformed American landscapes and economies. The exchange also carried Old World diseases such as smallpox and measles to populations with no prior exposure, with catastrophic results. Many historians regard it as a turning point in the history of global ecology and diet.

title: Demographic collapse of the Indigenous Americas
summary: Epidemics of smallpox, measles and other diseases, compounded by war, forced labour and famine, killed most of the Indigenous population of the Americas.
description: Populations with no prior exposure to Old World diseases suffered repeated epidemics: smallpox struck the Caribbean and Mexico in 1518–20 and reached the Andes by the late 1520s, and the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 devastated central Mexico. Violence, enslavement, forced labour, displacement and famine compounded the losses. Estimates of the population of the Americas in 1492 vary widely, from around 8 million to more than 100 million, but most scholars agree that numbers fell by roughly 80–90 percent in many regions within a century. Some researchers have linked the regrowth of forest on abandoned farmland to a dip in atmospheric carbon dioxide around 1610, a proposal that remains debated.

title: Cabral reaches Brazil
summary: A Portuguese fleet bound for India under Pedro Álvares Cabral sighted the coast of Brazil and claimed it for Portugal.
description: Following Vasco da Gama's route to India, Cabral's 13-ship fleet swung far west into the Atlantic and sighted Monte Pascoal on 22 April 1500, landing near present-day Porto Seguro in Bahia. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 the land lay within Portugal's sphere. Whether the landfall was accidental or planned is still debated by historians. Brazil, named after the brazilwood traded from its coast, was later colonised for sugar production using enslaved Indigenous and African labour and became Portugal's largest colony.

title: The transatlantic slave trade
summary: Over three and a half centuries about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas; about 10.7 million survived the crossing.
description: Enslaved Africans were taken to Spanish Hispaniola from the first years of the 16th century, and direct voyages from Africa to the Americas began in the 1520s. The trade grew enormously with the sugar plantations of Brazil and the Caribbean and later supplied the tobacco, rice and cotton economies of North America. According to the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, about 12.5 million people embarked, the largest numbers from West Central Africa around Luanda and from the Bight of Benin, and some 1.8 million died during the Middle Passage. Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried the most captives, followed by British, French, Spanish and Dutch traders. Britain and the United States banned the trade in 1807–08, but illegal voyages continued until the 1860s; the trade reshaped African states, enriched Europe and the Americas, and created the African diaspora.

title: Ismail I founds Safavid Iran
summary: Shah Ismail I took Tabriz and proclaimed Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, founding the Safavid dynasty that shaped modern Iran.
description: Ismail, the teenage head of the Safavid Sufi order, led his Qizilbash Turkmen followers to victory over the Aq Qoyunlu and was crowned shah at Tabriz in 1501. He made Twelver Shi'ism the official religion, beginning a conversion of Iran's largely Sunni population that took generations. Defeat by the Ottomans at Chaldiran in 1514 checked Safavid expansion westward and began a long rivalry between the two empires. Under Shah Abbas I (1588–1629), who moved the capital to Isfahan, the empire reached its political and cultural height. The dynasty effectively fell after Afghan invaders captured Isfahan in 1722.

title: Afonso I of Kongo and the Portuguese
summary: King Afonso I made Kongo a Christian kingdom allied with Portugal, but his letters protested against Portuguese slavers seizing his subjects.
description: Kongo, a powerful kingdom on the lower Congo River in today's Angola and Democratic Republic of the Congo, had been in contact with Portugal since 1483. Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga), a convert to Catholicism, won a succession struggle and promoted Christianity, literacy and Portuguese-style titles, sending young nobles to study in Lisbon; his son Henrique was named a bishop in 1518. In letters to the Portuguese king in 1526, Afonso complained that traders were kidnapping free Kongolese, including nobles, and tried to regulate the slave trade. Kongo remained an independent Christian kingdom for centuries, though weakened by civil wars and the slave trade.

title: Portugal seizes Goa: the Estado da Índia
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate, giving Portugal the future capital of a maritime empire of fortified ports from Mozambique to Macau.
description: Vasco da Gama's voyage to Calicut in 1498 opened a direct sea route from Europe to India, and Portugal quickly set out to control the Indian Ocean spice trade by force. Under the first viceroy, Francisco de Almeida, and the governor Afonso de Albuquerque, the Portuguese defeated a Mamluk–Gujarati fleet at Diu in 1509 and seized Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515). The resulting Estado da Índia was a network of forts and trading posts rather than a territorial empire, taxing Asian shipping through a system of passes called cartazes. Goa became its capital in 1530, replacing Cochin, and remained a centre of Catholic missions and Portuguese rule until India annexed it in 1961.

title: Piri Reis map and the 'ice-free Antarctica' claim
dateLabel: Map drawn 1513; claim popularised from the 1960s
summary: Some writers claim the 1513 world map of Ottoman admiral Piri Reis shows Antarctica's coast free of ice, copied from a lost ancient civilisation.
description: The surviving fragment of Piri Reis's world map, rediscovered in Istanbul's Topkapı Palace in 1929, shows the Atlantic coasts of Europe, Africa and South America and is one of the oldest surviving maps to show the Americas; its notes say it was compiled from about twenty sources, including a map by Columbus. In 1966 the historian Charles Hapgood argued in Maps of the Ancient Sea Kings that its southern coastline depicts Queen Maud Land in Antarctica as it looked before glaciation, implying an advanced lost civilisation that had mapped the world. The idea was taken up by Erich von Däniken and Graham Hancock and is widely repeated in popular media.
mainstreamView: Historians of cartography read the southern coast as the South American coastline bent eastward to fit the parchment, a common distortion in maps compiled from several sources, and its details do not match Antarctica's subglacial topography. The coast of Queen Maud Land has been ice-covered for millions of years, long before humans existed, so no one could have surveyed it free of ice. The map's own notes name its Portuguese, Arab and Columbian sources, and Antarctica was not sighted by anyone until 1820.

title: Ottomans conquer the Mamluk Sultanate
summary: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya and took Cairo, adding Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia to the Ottoman Empire.
description: Fresh from his victory over Safavid Iran at Chaldiran in 1514, the Ottoman sultan Selim I turned on the Mamluk Sultanate, which had ruled Egypt and Syria since 1250. His army, with field artillery and Janissary musketeers, routed the Mamluk cavalry at Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo in August 1516, where Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri died, and defeated his successor Tumanbay II at Ridaniya outside Cairo in January 1517. Cairo fell after days of street fighting, and Tumanbay was captured and hanged at one of the city's gates in April. The conquest gave the Ottomans the grain and revenues of Egypt, control of the Red Sea routes and the role of protector of Mecca and Medina, transforming a mainly Anatolian and Balkan state into the leading power of the Islamic world. The last Abbasid caliph of Cairo was taken to Istanbul, and a much later tradition claimed he had passed the caliphate to the Ottoman sultans.

title: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther's theses against the sale of indulgences, spread by the printing press, sparked the Protestant Reformation and split Western Christianity.
description: Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and theology professor at Wittenberg, wrote 95 propositions criticising the sale of indulgences, which were being promoted to fund the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica in Rome. Whether he actually nailed them to the door of the Castle Church is debated, since the story first appears in an account by Philip Melanchthon written after Luther's death, but he did send them to Archbishop Albert of Mainz on 31 October 1517. Printed copies spread across the German lands within weeks. Luther's break with Rome, confirmed by his excommunication and his refusal to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, launched the Protestant Reformation, which reshaped religion, politics and education across Europe.

title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
summary: Hernán Cortés and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, aided by a smallpox epidemic, besieged and took Tenochtitlan, ending Mexica rule.
description: Hernán Cortés landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred Spanish soldiers and allied with the Totonacs and Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Mexica (Aztec) Triple Alliance. Received in Tenochtitlan by Moctezuma II, the Spaniards took him hostage; after his death they were driven from the city in 1520 on the 'Noche Triste'. A smallpox epidemic then killed many of the city's inhabitants, including the new ruler Cuitláhuac. After a siege of about three months, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, and Mexico City was built on its ruins as the capital of New Spain. Recent historians emphasise that Indigenous allies supplied most of the fighting force and that the conquest was a long process extending well beyond 1521.

title: Magellan–Elcano expedition circles the globe
summary: Of five ships and about 270 men who sailed under Magellan, only the Victoria, under Elcano with 18 survivors, completed the first circumnavigation.
description: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in Spanish service, sought a western route to the Spice Islands. His fleet found the strait at the southern tip of South America that now bears his name in late 1520 and crossed the Pacific, which proved far wider than expected, reaching the Philippines in March 1521. Magellan was killed at the Battle of Mactan in April 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano led the Victoria home across the Indian Ocean and around Africa, arriving at Sanlúcar de Barrameda in September 1522. The voyage revealed the true size of the Pacific and demonstrated that the world's oceans are connected.

title: Reign of Suleiman the Magnificent
summary: Under Suleiman I the Ottoman Empire took Belgrade, Rhodes, Baghdad and most of Hungary and besieged Vienna, reaching the height of its power.
description: Suleiman I succeeded his father Selim I, who had conquered Mamluk Syria and Egypt in 1516–17. His armies captured Belgrade (1521) and Rhodes (1522), crushed the Hungarian army at Mohács (1526) and besieged Vienna in 1529, while campaigns against Safavid Iran won Baghdad in 1534. Ottoman fleets under Hayreddin Barbarossa dominated the Mediterranean. Known in Turkish as Kanuni, 'the Lawgiver', Suleiman oversaw legal codification and a cultural flowering whose emblem is the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul by the architect Mimar Sinan. He died during the siege of Szigetvár in 1566.

title: Babur founds the Mughal Empire at Panipat
summary: Babur, a Timurid prince ruling from Kabul, used field guns and matchlocks to defeat Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi, founding the Mughal Empire.
description: Babur, descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, had lost his Central Asian homeland of Fergana and ruled from Kabul when he invaded the Delhi Sultanate. At Panipat his army of perhaps 12,000–25,000 men, combining a barricade of carts, artillery and mounted archers, defeated a much larger force under Ibrahim Lodi, who was killed in the battle. Victory over a Rajput confederacy at Khanwa in 1527 consolidated the conquest. The Mughal dynasty he founded came to rule most of the Indian subcontinent and was among the wealthiest states in the world in the 16th and 17th centuries.

title: Ethiopian–Adal War
summary: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim of Adal overran much of Christian Ethiopia until an Ethiopian–Portuguese army defeated and killed him in 1543.
description: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, known in Ethiopia as Gragn ('the left-handed'), led the Sultanate of Adal, based at Harar, in a holy war against the Ethiopian Empire, winning at Shimbra Kure in 1529 and later aided by firearms and Ottoman musketeers. His forces conquered most of the Ethiopian highlands, destroying many churches and monasteries. In 1541 about 400 Portuguese musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama, a son of Vasco da Gama, landed to aid Emperor Gelawdewos; da Gama was captured and killed, but at Wayna Daga near Lake Tana in 1543 the allies defeated and killed the imam. Both states emerged exhausted, opening the way for large-scale Oromo migrations into the highlands.

title: Pizarro captures Atahualpa at Cajamarca
summary: Francisco Pizarro's small force seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca, beginning the Spanish conquest of the largest state in the Americas.
description: Francisco Pizarro arrived in Peru as the Inca Empire, already weakened by smallpox, was emerging from a civil war between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar. At Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 about 170 Spaniards ambushed Atahualpa's retinue and captured him; he paid a huge ransom in gold and silver but was executed in 1533. The Spaniards took Cusco later that year, founded Lima in 1535 and survived a major rebellion led by Manco Inca in 1536–37. A neo-Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572, when its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, was captured and executed. The conquest brought Andean labour and silver under Spanish rule for nearly three centuries.

title: Henry VIII breaks with Rome
summary: Denied an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England with the Act of Supremacy.
description: Henry VIII wanted to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, who had not produced a surviving son, but Pope Clement VII, under pressure from Catherine's nephew Emperor Charles V, refused. Henry married Anne Boleyn in 1533, and Parliament cut ties with Rome in a series of acts culminating in the Act of Supremacy of 1534. Between 1536 and 1541 the crown dissolved England's monasteries and seized their wealth. Doctrine swung between Catholic and Protestant positions under Henry's children Edward VI and Mary I before Elizabeth I's settlement of 1559 established a lasting Protestant Church of England.

title: Copernicus proposes a Sun-centred cosmos
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus, printed in the year of his death, placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the planetary system.
description: Copernicus, a canon of Frombork (Frauenburg) Cathedral in Royal Prussia, had circulated an outline of heliocentrism before 1514 in his Commentariolus. His full treatise, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, was printed in Nuremberg in 1543, with an unsigned preface by the theologian Andreas Osiander presenting it as a mere calculating device. The model explained the retrograde motion of the planets as a consequence of Earth's own orbit, though it still used circular orbits and epicycles and was no more accurate than Ptolemy's. Its acceptance was slow, but it laid the groundwork for Kepler, Galileo and Newton and is often taken as the start of the Scientific Revolution.

title: Vesalius publishes De humani corporis fabrica
summary: Andreas Vesalius's lavishly illustrated anatomy, based on his own dissections, corrected many errors inherited from the ancient physician Galen.
description: Vesalius, a Flemish physician teaching at the University of Padua, performed dissections himself rather than leaving them to assistants, and found that many of Galen's descriptions were based on animals rather than humans. His seven-book Fabrica, printed in Basel in 1543, the same year as Copernicus's De revolutionibus, combined detailed text with woodcuts of exceptional quality attributed to artists of Titian's circle, possibly Jan van Calcar. It established direct observation as the basis of anatomy and is regarded as a foundation of modern medicine.
