title: Silver strike at Potosí
summary: The discovery of the Cerro Rico silver mountain in Upper Peru created one of the largest cities in the world and a flood of silver into the global economy.
description: Silver was found at Cerro Rico in 1545, and Potosí, in today's Bolivia, grew to perhaps 160,000 people by the early 17th century. Production soared from the 1570s with the mercury amalgamation process, using mercury from Huancavelica, and with the mita, a forced-labour draft that compelled Andean communities to send workers to the mines under brutal conditions. Together with the Mexican mines, Potosí made Spanish America the source of most of the world's silver in the 16th–18th centuries. Much of that silver flowed to Europe and, via Manila and European traders, to China, whose tax system had shifted to payment in silver.

title: Council of Trent
summary: Meeting in three periods over 18 years, the Council of Trent defined Catholic doctrine against Protestantism and launched the Counter-Reformation.
description: Summoned by Pope Paul III, the council met at Trento in northern Italy in three periods between 1545 and 1563. It reaffirmed Catholic teaching on scripture and tradition, justification, the seven sacraments and transubstantiation, rejecting Protestant positions, while also reforming abuses: bishops were required to reside in their dioceses and seminaries were established to train priests. Its decrees, together with new orders such as the Jesuits (approved in 1540), shaped the Catholic Counter-Reformation and the Church's worldwide missions. The Tridentine liturgy and catechism that followed remained standard until the Second Vatican Council in the 1960s.

title: Ivan IV crowned first Tsar of All Russia
summary: Grand Prince Ivan IV of Moscow was crowned tsar, conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and opened the way to Siberia, but his later rule became a reign of terror.
description: Ivan IV, grand prince since the age of three, was crowned in the Kremlin's Dormition Cathedral as the first Tsar of All Russia. His early reign brought legal and church reforms and the conquest of the khanates of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556), commemorated by St Basil's Cathedral, giving Russia control of the Volga. From 1565 his oprichnina, a state within the state, carried out purges and massacres such as the sack of Novgorod in 1570, and in 1581 he killed his own son and heir in a rage. The Cossack Yermak's expedition of 1581–82, backed by the Stroganov merchants, began the Russian conquest of Siberia.

title: Nostradamus's prophecies
summary: Supporters claim the French physician Nostradamus's 1555 book of rhyming quatrains accurately foretold events from the Great Fire of London to Hitler.
description: Michel de Nostredame, a physician and astrologer living in Salon-de-Provence, published Les Prophéties in 1555, a collection of four-line verses in French mixed with Latin and other languages, expanded in later editions to nearly a thousand quatrains. His almanacs and horoscopes won him the patronage of Queen Catherine de' Medici. Since his death in 1566, interpreters have claimed that the quatrains predicted the death of Henry II, the Great Fire of London, the French Revolution, Napoleon, Adolf Hitler and the 11 September attacks, and new interpretations appear after most major world events.
mainstreamView: Scholars regard the quatrains as deliberately obscure verse drawing on earlier prophetic, astrological and classical sources. They contain almost no dates and use vague imagery, so interpreters can match them to events only after the fact, and no quatrain has ever been used to predict a specific event in advance. Supposed hits often depend on mistranslation or altered text, such as reading 'Hister', a classical name for the lower Danube, as Hitler, and several widely shared 'prophecies' are outright fabrications.

title: 1556 Shaanxi earthquake
summary: The deadliest earthquake in recorded history killed about 830,000 people in Shaanxi and neighbouring provinces of Ming China.
description: The earthquake struck near Hua County in the Wei River valley during the reign of the Jiajing Emperor, and modern seismologists estimate its magnitude at around 8. Official Ming records give a death toll of about 830,000, a figure that cannot be independently verified but is generally accepted as the highest for any earthquake. Many victims lived in yaodong, artificial caves dug into the soft loess cliffs of the Loess Plateau, which collapsed. The scholar Qin Keda, who survived, advised people to leave buildings quickly at the first tremors, one of the earliest recorded pieces of earthquake-safety advice.

title: Reign of Akbar the Great
summary: Akbar expanded the Mughal Empire across northern India, reformed taxation and government, and promoted tolerance among his diverse subjects.
description: Akbar came to the throne at 13 after the death of his father Humayun, and his regent's victory at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 secured the dynasty. Through conquest and alliances with Rajput rulers he extended Mughal rule from Afghanistan to Bengal and into the Deccan. His administration of ranked officials (mansabdars) and a land-revenue system based on measured fields endured for generations. Akbar abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, hosted debates among Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Christian scholars at his new city of Fatehpur Sikri, and promoted a syncretic court cult, the Din-i Ilahi. His reign is regarded as a high point of Mughal power and culture.

title: Reign of Elizabeth I
summary: Elizabeth I restored Protestantism in England, survived Catholic plots and the Armada, and presided over a flowering of drama and overseas ventures.
description: The daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, Elizabeth succeeded her Catholic half-sister Mary I and established a moderate Protestant Church of England with the settlement of 1559. She never married, using the prospect of marriage as a diplomatic tool, and became known as the Virgin Queen. Her reign saw conflict with Spain, the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587, privateering voyages such as Francis Drake's circumnavigation of 1577–80, the brutal conquest of Ireland and the chartering of the East India Company in 1600. The theatre of Marlowe and Shakespeare flourished, and her death ended the Tudor dynasty.

title: The Manila galleon trade
summary: Spanish galleons sailing between Manila and Acapulco carried American silver to Asia and Chinese silk and porcelain to the Americas.
description: In 1565 the navigator Andrés de Urdaneta found a return route from the Philippines to Mexico by sailing north to catch the westerlies, making regular trans-Pacific trade possible. After Miguel López de Legazpi founded Spanish Manila in 1571, one or two galleons a year crossed between Manila and Acapulco, exchanging Mexican and Peruvian silver for Chinese silk, porcelain and other Asian goods brought by Chinese merchants. Some historians date the beginning of truly global trade to 1571, when all the populated continents became continuously linked by trade. The route operated for some 250 years until 1815.

title: Dutch Revolt and the Eighty Years' War
summary: The Habsburg Netherlands rose against Philip II of Spain; the northern provinces formed the Dutch Republic, whose independence Spain recognised in 1648.
description: Heavy taxation, centralising rule from Madrid and the persecution of Protestants under Philip II provoked the iconoclastic riots of 1566, and the harsh repression that followed under the Duke of Alba drove nobles led by William of Orange into armed revolt in 1568. In 1572 the rebel privateers known as the Sea Beggars seized Brielle and most towns in Holland and Zeeland went over to the revolt, and in 1574 Leiden withstood a long Spanish siege. The northern provinces bound themselves together in the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and renounced Philip's sovereignty in the Act of Abjuration of 1581, while Spanish armies under the Duke of Parma reconquered the south, the future Belgium, taking Antwerp in 1585. After the Twelve Years' Truce (1609–1621) the war resumed alongside the Thirty Years' War until the Peace of Münster of 1648 recognised the independent Dutch Republic, by then the leading commercial power of its Golden Age.

title: Battle of Lepanto
summary: A Holy League fleet led by Don John of Austria destroyed most of the Ottoman fleet off western Greece in one of the largest galley battles in history.
description: Formed by Pope Pius V with Spain, Venice and other Catholic states after the Ottoman invasion of Venetian Cyprus, the Holy League fleet of more than 200 galleys and six Venetian galleasses met a similar Ottoman force under Ali Pasha at the mouth of the Gulf of Patras. The galleasses' firepower and Christian infantry overwhelmed the Ottomans, who lost most of their ships and tens of thousands of men; Miguel de Cervantes was among the wounded. The victory was celebrated across Catholic Europe, but its strategic effect was limited: the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year and kept Cyprus, which Venice formally ceded in 1573.

title: Gregorian calendar introduced
summary: Pope Gregory XIII reformed the Julian calendar, dropping ten days and refining the leap-year rule, creating the calendar used worldwide today.
description: The Julian calendar's year was about 11 minutes longer than the solar year, so by the 16th century the spring equinox had drifted ten days from 21 March, affecting the date of Easter. Based on proposals by the physician Aloysius Lilius and the astronomer Christopher Clavius, the papal bull Inter gravissimas decreed that Thursday 4 October 1582 would be followed by Friday 15 October, and that century years would be leap years only if divisible by 400. Catholic countries adopted it at once, but Protestant and Orthodox states followed slowly: Britain and its colonies in 1752, Russia in 1918 and Greece in 1923. It is now the international civil calendar.

title: Defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II's invasion fleet was broken up by fireships off Calais, beaten at Gravelines and wrecked by storms off Scotland and Ireland.
description: Philip II of Spain launched an Armada of about 130 ships to carry the Duke of Parma's army from Flanders to England, in response to English support for the Dutch revolt, privateering and the execution of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots. After running fights in the Channel, English fireships broke the Spanish formation off Calais and the fleet was mauled at the Battle of Gravelines. Unable to return through the Channel, the Armada sailed around Scotland and Ireland, where storms wrecked many ships; around a third of the ships and perhaps half the men were lost. The defeat became a founding legend of Elizabethan England, though the Anglo-Spanish War continued until 1604 and Spain rebuilt its navy.

title: Shakespeare authorship question
dateLabel: Plays written c. 1590–1613; doubts raised from the 1850s
summary: Some argue that the works attributed to William Shakespeare were really written by Edward de Vere, Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe or another writer.
description: Doubts about Shakespeare's authorship were first voiced in the mid-19th century, notably by Delia Bacon, who promoted Francis Bacon as the true author. Proponents argue that a glover's son from Stratford-upon-Avon with a grammar-school education could not have acquired the knowledge of courts, law and foreign lands shown in the plays, and point out that few personal documents survive. Since J. Thomas Looney's book of 1920, the leading candidate has been Edward de Vere, 17th Earl of Oxford; others include Christopher Marlowe and William Stanley, Earl of Derby. Supporters have included well-known actors and judges, keeping the question in public view.
mainstreamView: Virtually all Shakespeare scholars and historians accept that William Shakespeare of Stratford wrote the works attributed to him. His name appears on title pages and in contemporary records as a playwright, fellow writers such as Ben Jonson praised him as author, and the First Folio of 1623 links him to Stratford through its 'Sweet Swan of Avon' tribute and the monument there. De Vere died in 1604, before plays such as Macbeth and The Tempest are generally dated, and stylistic analysis confirms Shakespeare's documented collaborations with John Fletcher and Thomas Middleton. A lack of personal papers is normal for commoners of the period, and the anti-Stratfordian case rests on assumptions about class and education rather than documentary evidence.

title: Moroccan invasion topples the Songhai Empire
summary: A Moroccan army armed with arquebuses and cannon crossed the Sahara and routed the much larger Songhai army at Tondibi, ending West Africa's largest empire.
description: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco coveted the gold and salt trade of the western Sudan and sent an army of about 4,000 men, many of them Spanish-born converts and Andalusian exiles, across the Sahara under the pasha Judar. At Tondibi near Gao the forces of Askia Ishaq II, far more numerous but armed mainly with spears and bows, were defeated by gunpowder weapons. The Moroccans occupied Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné, but the occupation proved costly and the gold supply disappointing. The fall of Songhai fragmented the Niger bend region politically and coincided with a shift of West African trade from the Sahara toward the Atlantic coast.

title: Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War)
summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's armies invaded Korea, but Korean resistance, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy and Ming Chinese intervention drove them back.
description: Having unified Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi sent some 150,000 troops to invade Joseon Korea in 1592 as a first step toward conquering Ming China. The Japanese landed at Busan and quickly took Seoul and Pyongyang, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's fleet, including a few covered, spiked 'turtle ships' (geobukseon), cut their supply lines by sea, while Korean irregular 'righteous armies' harassed them on land. Ming China sent large armies from 1593, and after stalemate and failed negotiations a second invasion in 1597 was confined to the south. The Japanese withdrew after Hideyoshi's death in 1598. The war devastated Korea and strained Ming finances, and thousands of Korean captives, notably potters, were taken to Japan.

title: Shakespeare's plays at the Globe
summary: In Elizabethan and Jacobean London, William Shakespeare wrote plays such as Hamlet, Othello and King Lear for his company's new Globe Theatre.
description: Born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, Shakespeare was an actor, shareholder and playwright with the Lord Chamberlain's Men (later the King's Men), who built the Globe on Bankside in 1599 from the timbers of an earlier playhouse. Over about 25 years he wrote or co-wrote some 38 plays and 154 sonnets, among them Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Othello, King Lear and Macbeth, several first performed at the Globe. Seven years after his death in 1616, his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 plays in the First Folio, preserving 18 that had never been printed. His works, translated into every major language, are among the most performed in world drama and profoundly shaped modern English.

title: Huaynaputina eruption
summary: The largest volcanic eruption in recorded South American history buried villages in southern Peru and cooled the Northern Hemisphere's climate.
description: Huaynaputina, a volcano with no previously recorded activity, erupted explosively for about two weeks in February and March 1600 in a VEI 6 event. Ash and pyroclastic flows destroyed villages and buried the fields and vineyards of the Arequipa region, killing at least 1,500 people. Sulphate aerosols cooled the Northern Hemisphere, and tree rings show 1601 as one of the coldest summers of the past six centuries. The eruption has been linked to the Russian famine of 1601–1603, which killed a large part of the population and contributed to the Time of Troubles.

title: Matteo Ricci reaches Beijing
summary: The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci was permitted to live in Beijing, opening a long exchange between Chinese and European learning.
description: Ricci arrived in Macau in 1582 and with Michele Ruggieri settled at Zhaoqing, learning classical Chinese and eventually adopting the dress of a Confucian scholar. After years in southern cities he reached Beijing in 1601, where gifts including clocks won him the Wanli Emperor's favour and permission to reside in the capital, and he became the first European known to enter the Forbidden City. He produced a world map in Chinese, translated Euclid with the convert Xu Guangqi, and argued that Confucian rites were compatible with Christianity, an approach later rejected by Rome in the Chinese Rites controversy. Jesuits after him served the Ming and Qing courts as astronomers for more than a century.

title: Dutch East India Company (VOC)
summary: The Dutch East India Company, an early joint-stock firm with publicly traded shares, built a trading empire in Asia ruled from Batavia on Java.
description: Chartered by the States General in 1602 with a monopoly on Dutch trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, the VOC raised capital from the public and its shares traded on the Amsterdam exchange, making it a pioneer of the modern corporation. It could wage war, make treaties and govern territory: under Jan Pieterszoon Coen it founded Batavia (now Jakarta) in 1619 and violently seized control of the nutmeg and clove trade of the Banda and Maluku Islands. The company was central to the wealth of the Dutch Golden Age, operating posts from the Cape to Nagasaki. Burdened by debt and corruption, it was nationalised in 1796 and dissolved at the end of 1799.

title: Tokugawa shogunate established
summary: After victory at Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun, beginning more than 250 years of peace and centralised rule from Edo.
description: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeated a rival coalition of daimyo at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, ending more than a century of civil war that Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi had largely brought under control. Appointed shogun by the emperor in 1603, he governed from Edo (now Tokyo), and in 1614–15 he and his son Hidetada, the second shogun, destroyed the Toyotomi at Osaka. The regime controlled the daimyo through the system of alternate attendance, banned Christianity and from the 1630s sharply restricted foreign contact. The long Edo-period peace brought rapid urban growth, with Edo becoming one of the world's largest cities, and a flourishing popular culture. The shogunate lasted until the Meiji Restoration of 1868.

title: Cervantes publishes Don Quixote
summary: Miguel de Cervantes's comic tale of a gentleman who believes himself a knight-errant is often called the first modern novel.
description: Published in Madrid in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha follows Alonso Quixano, who has read so many chivalric romances that he sets out with his squire Sancho Panza to right the world's wrongs. Its interplay of illusion and reality, its many voices and its self-aware narration, including characters in Part Two who have read Part One, have led many critics to call it the first modern novel. Cervantes, a veteran wounded at Lepanto who spent five years as a captive in Algiers, died in 1616. The book became one of the most translated works of literature and a pillar of the Spanish Golden Age.

title: Jamestown founded
summary: The Virginia Company founded Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in the Americas, in the territory of the Powhatan Confederacy.
description: About 104 colonists landed on a marshy island in the James River in May 1607. Disease, poor water and conflict with the Powhatan Confederacy killed most of them, and the winter of 1609–10 became known as the 'Starving Time'. The colony survived thanks to supply fleets and, from 1612, the export of tobacco introduced by John Rolfe, who married Pocahontas in 1614. In 1619 Virginia convened the first elected representative assembly in English America, and the same year the first recorded enslaved Africans arrived. Jamestown was the starting point of English colonisation of North America and of a long series of wars with Indigenous nations.

title: Voynich manuscript and its fringe 'solutions'
summary: An undeciphered illustrated codex reportedly owned by Emperor Rudolf II has drawn claims of alien or lost-civilisation origin and many announced 'solutions'.
description: The manuscript, named after the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who acquired it in 1912, and now held by Yale's Beinecke Library, has about 240 vellum pages of an unknown script with drawings of unidentified plants, astronomical diagrams and bathing women. Its earliest documented owners lived in Prague in the 17th century: a letter of the 1660s sent with it to the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher reports a claim that Emperor Rudolf II had bought it for 600 ducats, and a faded name on the first page has been read as that of Rudolf's physician Jacobus Horčický de Tepenec. Fringe writers have attributed it to extraterrestrials, survivors of Atlantis or another lost civilisation, or secret knowledge encoded by the 13th-century friar Roger Bacon. Confident 'decipherments' as abbreviated Latin, 'proto-Romance', Hebrew, Turkish and other languages appear regularly in books and the press.
mainstreamView: Radiocarbon dating of the vellum in 2009 placed it in 1404–1438, long after Roger Bacon's death in 1292, and its pigments are consistent with that period; its plant, zodiac and bathing illustrations fit 15th-century European, possibly Italian, manuscript traditions. Scholars still genuinely debate whether the text records a natural language, a cipher or a constructed system, or is meaningless, but every announced solution has been rejected by specialists because it cannot be applied consistently to the whole text. Nothing in the manuscript points to non-human or lost-civilisation origins.

title: Kepler's laws of planetary motion
summary: Using Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars, Johannes Kepler showed that planets move in ellipses, sweeping out equal areas in equal times.
description: As imperial mathematician in Prague, Kepler inherited the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, who died in 1601. Years of calculation on the orbit of Mars led him to abandon the ancient assumption of circular motion: Astronomia nova (1609) set out his first two laws, that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus and that a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Harmonices Mundi (1619) added the third law, relating a planet's orbital period to its distance from the Sun. His Rudolphine Tables of 1627 were far more accurate than earlier tables, and Newton later explained all three laws by universal gravitation.

title: Galileo turns a telescope to the sky
summary: Galileo's improved telescope revealed mountains on the Moon, four moons of Jupiter and countless stars, discoveries he published in Sidereus Nuncius.
description: After hearing of a Dutch spyglass presented to the States General in 1608, Galileo Galilei, then a professor at Padua, built telescopes magnifying up to about 20 times. Between late 1609 and early 1610 he observed mountains and craters on the Moon, resolved the Milky Way into stars and discovered four satellites orbiting Jupiter, which he named the Medicean stars. His later observations of the full cycle of phases of Venus were incompatible with the Ptolemaic system, though not with Tycho Brahe's hybrid model. Sidereus Nuncius made Galileo famous and turned the telescope into a scientific instrument.

title: The Thirty Years' War
summary: A Bohemian revolt grew into a war that drew in most European powers, ravaged the Holy Roman Empire and killed several million people.
description: The war began when Protestant nobles threw imperial officials from a window of Prague Castle in 1618, rebelling against the Catholic Habsburg Ferdinand II. What started as a religious and constitutional conflict within the Holy Roman Empire drew in Denmark, Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus and Catholic France, which fought the Habsburgs for dynastic and strategic rather than religious reasons. Armies living off the land, together with famine and plague, caused deaths estimated at 4.5 to 8 million, and some regions of Germany lost more than half their population. The war ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, though the Franco-Spanish war continued until 1659.

title: Mayflower Pilgrims found Plymouth Colony
summary: English religious Separatists aboard the Mayflower settled at Plymouth in Massachusetts after signing the Mayflower Compact for self-government.
description: The Pilgrims, Separatists from the Church of England who had lived for a time in Leiden, sailed with other colonists on the Mayflower in 1620. Having landed outside the area of their patent, 41 men signed the Mayflower Compact agreeing to form a 'civil body politic'. About half the settlers died in the first winter; the survivors were helped by the Wampanoag sachem Massasoit and by Tisquantum (Squanto), and their 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag was later popularised, mainly in the 19th century, as the 'First Thanksgiving'. Plymouth was followed by the much larger Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1630, and relations with Native nations later collapsed into King Philip's War of 1675–76.

title: Queen Nzinga resists Portuguese Angola
summary: Nzinga Mbande, ruler of Ndongo and Matamba, fought and negotiated with the Portuguese for four decades to keep her kingdoms independent.
description: Nzinga first came to prominence in 1622 as her brother's envoy to the Portuguese governor in Luanda, where she was baptised. After taking power in Ndongo around 1624, she faced Portuguese armies seeking captives for the slave trade, and in the 1630s she conquered the kingdom of Matamba and allied with Imbangala war bands. She sided with the Dutch during their occupation of Luanda in the 1640s and finally made peace with Portugal in 1656, ruling until her death in 1663. She is remembered in Angola as a symbol of resistance to colonial rule.

title: Harvey describes the circulation of the blood
summary: William Harvey showed by experiment and measurement that the heart pumps blood around the body in a continuous circuit.
description: Harvey, an English physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London who had studied at Padua, published De motu cordis in Frankfurt in 1628. Calculating that the heart pumps far more blood in an hour than the body could make from food, and using ligature experiments on veins and arteries, he concluded that the blood circulates, overturning Galen's view that it is continually produced by the liver and consumed by the body. He could not see how blood passed from arteries to veins; Marcello Malpighi observed the capillaries with a microscope in 1661, completing the picture.

title: The Taj Mahal is built
summary: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built a white marble mausoleum at Agra for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, a masterpiece of Indo-Islamic architecture.
description: Mumtaz Mahal died in childbirth in 1631, and Shah Jahan ordered a tomb on the bank of the Yamuna at Agra. The main mausoleum was largely completed by about 1643 and the surrounding garden, mosque, guest house and gateway by around 1653, employing some 20,000 workers under the architect usually identified as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. Its white Makrana marble is inlaid with semi-precious stones in floral and calligraphic designs. Shah Jahan, deposed by his son Aurangzeb in 1658, was buried beside his wife. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by millions of people every year.

title: Trial of Galileo
summary: The Roman Inquisition found Galileo 'vehemently suspect of heresy' for defending Copernicanism and confined him to house arrest for life.
description: In 1616 Church authorities condemned the claim that the Earth moves around the Sun as contrary to scripture, suspended Copernicus's book pending corrections and warned Galileo not to hold or defend the theory. His Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632) was seen as favouring Copernicus and as mocking Pope Urban VIII's views, leading to his trial in Rome. In June 1633 he was forced to abjure and sentenced to house arrest, which he spent at Arcetri near Florence, where he wrote his Two New Sciences. The affair became a lasting symbol of conflict between science and religious authority, though historians stress the roles of politics and personalities; Pope John Paul II acknowledged the Church's error in 1992.

title: Tulip mania
summary: Prices of rare tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic soared to extraordinary levels before collapsing suddenly in February 1637.
description: Tulips, introduced from the Ottoman Empire in the late 16th century, became luxury goods in the prosperous Dutch Republic, with rare 'broken' varieties, streaked by a mosaic virus, fetching the highest prices. In the winter of 1636–37 contracts for future delivery of bulbs were traded in taverns at rapidly rising prices, some single bulbs reportedly selling for more than a skilled craftsman earned in years, until buyers failed to appear at an auction in Haarlem in early February 1637. Long cited as the first speculative bubble, the episode has been reassessed by historians such as Anne Goldgar, who found little evidence of widespread ruin and argue that later moralising accounts greatly exaggerated its economic impact.

title: Japan's sakoku: closing the country
summary: The Tokugawa shogunate expelled the Portuguese and limited European trade to the Dutch at Dejima in Nagasaki, restricting foreign contact for two centuries.
description: Fearing Christianity as a threat to its authority, especially after the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637–38, the shogunate issued edicts in the 1630s forbidding Japanese to travel abroad and in 1639 expelled the Portuguese. From 1641 the Dutch were confined to the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour, while Chinese merchants traded at Nagasaki and relations with Korea, the Ryukyu Kingdom and the Ainu continued through intermediary domains. Historians now stress that Japan was regulated rather than sealed off, and Dutch books fed a school of 'Dutch learning' (rangaku) in science and medicine. The policy ended when US Commodore Matthew Perry forced Japan to open its ports in 1853–54.

title: English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
summary: Conflict between Charles I and Parliament led to civil wars, the king's trial and execution in 1649, and a republic dominated by Oliver Cromwell.
description: Disputes over taxation, religion and royal power, together with rebellions in Scotland and Ireland, led to war between Royalists and Parliamentarians in 1642. Parliament's New Model Army won decisively at Naseby in 1645, and after a second war Charles I was tried and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649. England became a Commonwealth; Oliver Cromwell conquered Ireland with great brutality and ruled as Lord Protector from 1653. The wars across England, Scotland and Ireland are estimated to have killed a larger share of the population than the First World War. The monarchy was restored under Charles II in 1660, but the conflict established that kings could not rule without Parliament.

title: Abel Tasman reaches Tasmania and New Zealand
summary: The Dutch navigator Abel Tasman became the first European known to reach Tasmania and New Zealand, where a clash with Māori cost four of his crew.
description: Sent by the VOC from Batavia to explore the 'Great South Land', Tasman sighted the west coast of Tasmania, which he named Van Diemen's Land, in November 1642. In December he reached the South Island of New Zealand, where Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri canoes attacked a ship's boat in Golden Bay, killing four Dutch sailors; he named the place Murderers' Bay and sailed on without landing. He went on to Tonga and Fiji. His voyage showed that Australia was not joined to a great southern continent, though no Europeans returned to New Zealand until Cook in 1769.

title: Fall of Beijing and the Qing conquest of China
summary: Rebels took Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself; Manchu armies then seized the capital and founded China's last imperial dynasty, the Qing.
description: The Ming dynasty, weakened by fiscal crisis, famine, epidemics and the cold of the Little Ice Age, fell when the rebel Li Zicheng captured Beijing in April 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor took his own life. The Ming general Wu Sangui then let Manchu armies through Shanhai Pass; together they defeated Li, and the Manchus occupied Beijing in June, proclaiming the young Shunzhi Emperor ruler of China. Conquest of the south took decades and met fierce Ming loyalist resistance, ending with the capture of Taiwan in 1683. The Qing ruled until 1912 and later extended China's borders into Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet.

title: Maunder Minimum and the Little Ice Age
summary: Sunspots almost vanished for 70 years during one of the coldest phases of the Little Ice Age, when frost fairs were held on London's frozen Thames.
description: Astronomers observing with the new telescopes recorded very few sunspots between about 1645 and 1715, a period later named after the solar astronomer Edward Walter Maunder. It coincided with some of the coldest decades of the Little Ice Age, a loosely defined cool period from roughly the 14th to the 19th century, when Alpine glaciers advanced and frost fairs were held on the frozen Thames. Climate scientists consider reduced solar output only a minor cause of the cooling; clusters of large volcanic eruptions and natural climate variability probably mattered more, and the cold was uneven in time and place. Historians such as Geoffrey Parker have linked the harsh weather of the 17th century to famines, rebellions and wars around the world, the so-called General Crisis.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: Treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück ended the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War, recognising Dutch and Swiss independence.
description: After years of negotiation among delegates of most European powers, the treaties of Osnabrück and Münster ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire, while the Peace of Münster, signed earlier in 1648, ended Spain's long war with the Dutch Republic. The settlement extended the 1555 principle that rulers could determine their territories' religion to include Calvinists, strengthened the autonomy of the German princes, and awarded territory to France and Sweden. It is often described as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states, although many historians now regard this 'Westphalian' interpretation as a later myth, since the treaties preserved the Empire and did not set out sovereignty as a principle.

title: Dutch found Cape Town
summary: Jan van Riebeeck set up a VOC supply station at the Cape of Good Hope, the start of European settlement in what is now South Africa.
description: The Dutch East India Company sent Jan van Riebeeck with about 90 people to build a fort and grow fresh food for ships sailing between Europe and Asia. Company employees were soon released as free burghers to farm, and the colony imported enslaved people from Madagascar, Mozambique, India and Southeast Asia. Expansion into the interior brought wars with the Khoekhoe, who lost land and cattle, and smallpox epidemics from 1713 devastated them. French Huguenots joined the settlers from 1688, and the Dutch spoken by settlers, enslaved people and Khoekhoe gradually developed into Afrikaans; Britain took over the colony in 1795 and permanently from 1806.

title: Reign of the Kangxi Emperor
summary: China's longest-reigning emperor consolidated Qing rule, crushed the Three Feudatories, annexed Taiwan and fixed the border with Russia.
description: Enthroned as a child in 1661, the Kangxi Emperor took personal power in 1669 and defeated the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (1673–81), led by former Ming generals in the south. His forces took Taiwan from the Zheng regime in 1683, fought the Zunghar Mongols, and agreed with Russia the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689), China's first treaty with a European state. A patron of learning, he sponsored the Kangxi Dictionary, employed Jesuit astronomers at court and issued an edict of toleration for Christianity in 1692. His 61-year reign began the 'High Qing' era of stability and population growth continued by his grandson, the Qianlong Emperor.

title: Shivaji crowned, founding the Maratha state
summary: The Maratha leader Shivaji, who had carved out a kingdom in the western Deccan from Bijapur and the Mughals, was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad.
description: Shivaji Bhonsle built a power base in the hill forts of the Western Ghats from the 1640s, using mobile light cavalry and guerrilla tactics against the Bijapur Sultanate and the Mughal Empire of Aurangzeb; he famously escaped from Mughal detention at Agra in 1666. His coronation at Raigad in 1674 proclaimed an independent kingdom with its own administration and navy. Aurangzeb spent the last quarter-century of his life campaigning in the Deccan against the Marathas, draining Mughal resources. In the 18th century the Maratha Confederacy, led by the Peshwas from Pune, became one of the dominant powers in India until its defeat by the British in 1818.

title: Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles
summary: The 'Sun King' Louis XIV made his vastly enlarged palace at Versailles the seat of government, a model of absolute monarchy across Europe.
description: Louis XIV, king from 1643 and ruling personally from 1661, transformed his father's hunting lodge at Versailles into an immense palace and gardens and moved the court and government there in 1682. Requiring the great nobles to attend him, he concentrated power in the crown and in a bureaucracy led by ministers such as Jean-Baptiste Colbert. His 72-year reign, the longest recorded of any European monarch, saw France become the leading power in Europe, but also costly wars and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, which drove some 200,000 Huguenots abroad. Versailles was imitated by courts from Spain to Russia.

title: Ottoman siege of Vienna repulsed
summary: A relief army led by the Polish king John III Sobieski broke the two-month Ottoman siege of Vienna, beginning the Ottoman retreat from Central Europe.
description: Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged the Habsburg capital from July 1683 with a large Ottoman army. On 12 September a combined force of Polish, Austrian and German troops attacked from the Kahlenberg heights, culminating in one of history's largest cavalry charges, led by the Polish winged hussars, and routed the besiegers. The defeat led to Kara Mustafa's execution and to the Great Turkish War, in which a Holy League recovered Hungary. By the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the Ottomans ceded most of Hungary and Transylvania, their first major territorial loss in Europe.

title: Newton publishes the Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's Principia set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, explaining planetary orbits, tides and falling bodies with one set of laws.
description: Written at Cambridge and published in London under the auspices of the Royal Society, at Edmond Halley's urging and expense, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica showed that the force that makes objects fall also keeps the Moon in its orbit. Newton derived Kepler's laws of planetary motion from an inverse-square law of gravitation and explained the tides, the precession of the equinoxes and the paths of comets. The work provided the framework of classical mechanics that dominated physics until the 20th century. Its publication also prompted a bitter priority dispute with Robert Hooke over the inverse-square law.

title: The Glorious Revolution
summary: William of Orange invaded England and James II fled; Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary and passed the Bill of Rights.
description: The Catholic James II's policies and the birth of a male heir in 1688 alarmed Protestant elites, who invited the Dutch stadtholder William of Orange, husband of James's daughter Mary, to intervene. William landed at Torbay with a large army in November 1688, and James fled to France. In February 1689 Parliament offered the throne jointly to William III and Mary II, and the Bill of Rights later that year limited royal power and barred Catholics from the throne. The revolution was largely bloodless in England but not in Ireland and Scotland, where Jacobite wars followed, including the Battle of the Boyne in 1690. It established parliamentary supremacy and is seen as a foundation of British constitutional monarchy.

title: Salem witch trials
summary: Accusations that began with girls' fits in Salem Village, Massachusetts, led to 19 people being hanged for witchcraft and another pressed to death.
description: Beginning in February 1692, several girls in Salem Village suffered fits that local ministers attributed to witchcraft, and accusations spread to more than 150 people across Essex County. A special court admitted 'spectral evidence', testimony about visions of the accused's spirits, and hanged 19 people, most of them women; Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to enter a plea, and several others died in jail. Criticism from ministers such as Increase Mather led Governor William Phips to halt the court, and the last trials ended in 1693. Historians have explained the episode through local factional disputes, frontier war anxiety and Puritan beliefs, and it became a byword for mass hysteria and unjust persecution.

title: Bank of England founded
summary: A private company was chartered to lend £1.2 million to William III's government, creating the Bank of England, later a model for central banks.
description: To finance the Nine Years' War against France, the Scottish merchant William Paterson and others proposed a joint-stock bank whose subscribers would lend the government £1.2 million in return for interest and the right to issue banknotes. Together with a national debt funded by taxes voted by Parliament, the bank helped Britain borrow more cheaply than its rivals, part of a 'financial revolution' that historians credit with underpinning British military and commercial power in the 18th century. The bank gradually took on central-banking roles such as lender of last resort in the 19th century and was nationalised in 1946.

title: Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa
summary: At Anandpur, the tenth Sikh Guru, Gobind Singh, initiated the Khalsa, a community of committed Sikhs bound by a code of conduct and the five Ks.
description: Guru Gobind Singh, whose father Guru Tegh Bahadur had been executed on the orders of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb in 1675, gathered Sikhs at Anandpur for the festival of Vaisakhi in 1699. According to tradition, he called for volunteers willing to give their heads and initiated the first five, the Panj Piare, with sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword. Initiated men took the name Singh and women Kaur, and members keep five articles of faith, including uncut hair and a steel bracelet. Before his death in 1708 the Guru declared that the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would thereafter be the eternal Guru.

title: Rise of the Asante Empire
summary: Under Osei Tutu and the priest Okomfo Anokye, Akan states united around the Golden Stool at Kumasi and defeated Denkyira, founding the Asante Empire.
description: Osei Tutu, ruler of Kumasi, forged a confederation of Akan states in the forest zone of present-day Ghana; tradition holds that the priest Okomfo Anokye called down the Golden Stool from the sky as the embodiment of the nation's unity. Victory over the overlord state of Denkyira at the Battle of Feyiase around 1701 made Asante independent and the dominant power of the region. Rich in gold and kola, the empire expanded through the 18th century and sold war captives into the Atlantic slave trade through the European forts of the Gold Coast. Asante fought a series of wars against Britain in the 19th century before being annexed in 1902; its king, the Asantehene, retains a ceremonial role in Ghana today.

title: War of the Spanish Succession
summary: A Grand Alliance fought France over Louis XIV's grandson inheriting Spain; the Utrecht settlement kept him as Philip V but barred any union of the two crowns.
description: The childless Charles II of Spain died in 1700, leaving his empire to Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV of France. Fearing a union of the French and Spanish crowns, England, the Dutch Republic and the Austrian Habsburgs, who backed Archduke Charles as king of Spain, formed a Grand Alliance, and war spread across Flanders, Germany, Italy, Spain and the colonies, where in North America it was known as Queen Anne's War. The allied commanders the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy won major victories such as Blenheim in Bavaria (1704), but Philip held Spain with Castilian support, and Britain lost interest in Charles after he became emperor in 1711. The Treaties of Utrecht (1713) and Rastatt (1714) recognised Philip V on condition that he renounce the French throne; Austria gained the Spanish Netherlands, Milan and Naples, and Britain gained Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and the asiento contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America. The settlement shaped the 18th-century European balance of power and marked Britain's rise as a leading power.

title: Peter the Great founds Saint Petersburg
summary: Tsar Peter I founded a new capital on the Baltic as his 'window on Europe', part of sweeping reforms that made Russia a European great power.
description: Peter I, who had toured western Europe in 1697–98, reorganised Russia's army, created a navy, government colleges, a Table of Ranks and new taxes, and pressed the nobility to adopt western dress and education. He founded Saint Petersburg on land captured from Sweden at the mouth of the Neva and made it the capital in 1712; tens of thousands of conscripted labourers built it in harsh conditions. Victory over Charles XII of Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 gave Russia the eastern Baltic coast, and Peter proclaimed himself emperor. His reforms remain both a model and a point of controversy in debates about Russian modernisation.

title: Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine
summary: Thomas Newcomen's steam engine near Dudley pumped water from a coal mine, the first practical machine to turn the heat of burning fuel into work.
description: Thomas Newcomen, an ironmonger from Dartmouth, built on earlier experiments by Denis Papin and Thomas Savery. His engine injected cold water into a cylinder full of steam, creating a partial vacuum so that atmospheric pressure drove down a piston connected to a pump. The first documented engine was erected in 1712 at a coal mine near Dudley Castle in the West Midlands. Although very inefficient, hundreds were built across Britain and Europe over the following century, draining coal, tin and copper mines and making deeper mining possible; James Watt's improvements later built directly on the design.

title: Dahomey conquers Ouidah
summary: King Agaja of Dahomey seized the slave-trading port of Ouidah, though Dahomey soon became a tributary of the powerful Oyo Empire.
description: Dahomey, a Fon kingdom founded in the 17th century with its capital at Abomey in present-day Benin, expanded to the coast under King Agaja, conquering Allada in 1724 and the kingdom of Hueda with its port of Ouidah in 1727. Ouidah was one of the busiest slave-trading ports in Africa, and the trade became central to the Dahomean state. The Oyo Empire, a Yoruba state to the north-east whose cavalry dominated the savanna, invaded Dahomey repeatedly and from 1730 forced it to pay annual tribute, which continued until the 1820s. Dahomey was known for its centralised administration and its female military units, and it remained independent until French conquest in 1894.

title: Linnaeus's Systema Naturae
summary: Carl Linnaeus published a system for classifying nature that, with his later two-part Latin names, became the basis of biological taxonomy.
description: The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus first published Systema Naturae in the Netherlands in 1735 as a short work classifying the animal, plant and mineral kingdoms in a nested hierarchy of class, order, genus and species. His Species Plantarum (1753) and the tenth edition of Systema Naturae (1758) consistently applied two-part names such as Homo sapiens, and these works are the formal starting points of botanical and zoological nomenclature. Students he sent abroad, his 'apostles', collected specimens worldwide, including Daniel Solander on Cook's first voyage. Linnaeus grouped species by shared characteristics; after Darwin, classification came to reflect evolutionary descent.

title: Nader Shah sacks Delhi
summary: The Persian ruler Nader Shah defeated the Mughal army at Karnal, massacred thousands in Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor.
description: Nader, a Turkoman general who had driven the Afghans from Iran and taken the crown himself in 1736, ending Safavid rule, invaded the weakened Mughal Empire. He crushed Muhammad Shah's army at Karnal in February 1739 and occupied Delhi; after an attack on his troops, a massacre on 22 March killed perhaps 20,000–30,000 inhabitants. He left with immense treasure, including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, reportedly enough to suspend taxes in Iran for three years. The invasion exposed the Mughals' decline and hastened the rise of regional powers such as the Marathas and, later, the British East India Company.

title: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie
summary: A 28-volume encyclopedia edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert gathered the knowledge and critical ideas of the French Enlightenment.
description: Begun as a translation of Ephraim Chambers's Cyclopaedia, the Encyclopédie grew into an original work of 17 volumes of text and 11 of plates, with contributions from Voltaire, Montesquieu, Rousseau and many others. It gave detailed attention to crafts and technology alongside philosophy, and its articles often criticised religious authority and arbitrary government, sometimes indirectly through cross-references. The French authorities suspended it in 1752 and revoked its licence in 1759, the year Pope Clement XIII condemned it, but publication continued, partly in secret. It became a symbol of the Enlightenment's ambition to spread reason and useful knowledge.

title: 1755 Lisbon earthquake
summary: A great earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed much of Lisbon on All Saints' Day, killing tens of thousands and shaking Enlightenment thought.
description: The earthquake, with an epicentre in the Atlantic south-west of Cape St Vincent and a magnitude estimated at between about 7.7 and 9, struck on the morning of a religious holiday when churches were full. A tsunami followed about 40 minutes later and fires burned for days; estimates of deaths in Lisbon range from about 12,000 to 50,000, with more in Morocco and southern Spain. The chief minister, later the Marquis of Pombal, directed the rebuilding of the Baixa district with earthquake-resistant timber frames and commissioned a survey of the effects, an early step toward seismology. The disaster prompted debate about divine providence, notably in Voltaire's Poem on the Lisbon Disaster and his novel Candide.

title: The Seven Years' War
summary: Fought in Europe, North America, India, West Africa and the Philippines, the war left Britain the dominant colonial power, taking New France.
description: Often called the first global war, it combined a European conflict, in which Prussia under Frederick II survived a coalition of Austria, France and Russia, with an Anglo-French struggle for empire that had begun in the Ohio valley in 1754. British victories included the capture of Quebec after the Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759 and the defeat of French forces in India. By the Treaty of Paris of 1763 France ceded Canada and its lands east of the Mississippi to Britain, having already passed western Louisiana to Spain, which in turn ceded Florida to Britain. The war's cost led Britain to tax its American colonies, contributing to the American Revolution, while French debts fed the crisis that led to 1789.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive's East India Company army defeated the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, after bribing his commander, beginning British rule in India.
description: Disputes over trade privileges and fortifications led Siraj ud-Daulah to seize the company's base at Calcutta in 1756; a company force under Robert Clive retook it and then marched against him. At Plassey (Palashi) the nawab's much larger army collapsed after Clive secretly arranged for the commander Mir Jafar to stand aside in return for the throne. The company installed Mir Jafar as a puppet ruler and extracted huge sums, and after the Battle of Buxar it gained the diwani, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, in 1765. Plassey is generally taken as the start of Company rule, which spread across the subcontinent until the British Crown took over in 1858.

title: The Industrial Revolution begins in Britain
summary: Mechanised textile mills, coal and steam power transformed Britain's economy, beginning a worldwide shift from agrarian to industrial societies.
description: From around the 1760s, inventions such as the spinning jenny, the water frame and the spinning mule mechanised cotton production, while improved steam engines and coke-smelted iron supplied power and materials. Britain's accessible coal, high wages relative to energy costs, colonial markets, banking system and patent law are among the factors historians cite to explain why it began there. Manchester, the first great factory city, grew rapidly as cotton mills concentrated workers and machinery. Growth was slow at first, and economic historians debate how sudden the change was, generally dating the first phase to about 1760–1840. Industrialisation later spread to Europe, North America and Japan and underlies both modern economic growth and the rise in fossil-fuel emissions.

title: Third Battle of Panipat
summary: The Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani crushed a huge Maratha army north of Delhi in one of the largest and bloodiest battles of the 18th century.
description: By the 1750s the Maratha Confederacy had extended its power to the Punjab, bringing it into conflict with Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan. At Panipat, Durrani's army, allied with the Rohilla Afghans and the Nawab of Awadh, defeated the Maratha force under Sadashivrao Bhau, and tens of thousands of soldiers and camp followers were killed in the battle and the massacres that followed. The defeat halted Maratha expansion in the north for a decade, and the resulting power vacuum in northern India is often seen as easing the rise of the British East India Company.

title: Catherine the Great
summary: A German-born princess who seized the Russian throne in a coup, Catherine II expanded the empire to the Black Sea and patronised the Enlightenment.
description: Catherine came to power by overthrowing her husband, Peter III, in 1762. She corresponded with Voltaire and Diderot, founded the Hermitage collection and the Smolny Institute for the education of girls, and convened a Legislative Commission in 1767 guided by her own Enlightenment-inspired Instruction. Wars against the Ottoman Empire won the northern Black Sea coast and led to the annexation of Crimea in 1783, and Russia took the largest share of Poland in the partitions. Yet serfdom was extended and intensified, and the Pugachev Rebellion of 1773–75, the largest peasant revolt in Russian history, was brutally suppressed.

title: Fall of Ayutthaya
summary: Burmese armies of the Konbaung dynasty captured and destroyed Ayutthaya, the Siamese capital for four centuries, but Siam quickly recovered under Taksin.
description: After a siege of more than a year, the forces of King Hsinbyushin of Burma took Ayutthaya, one of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities in Southeast Asia, burning much of it and deporting tens of thousands of captives. The Burmese were soon distracted by a Qing Chinese invasion of Burma. The general Taksin rallied Siamese forces, expelled the Burmese garrisons and ruled from Thonburi; in 1782 his successor Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty, which still reigns, and moved the capital to Bangkok. The ruins of Ayutthaya are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: James Cook's first Pacific voyage
summary: HMS Endeavour observed the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, then charted New Zealand and the east coast of Australia for Britain.
description: The Royal Society and the Admiralty sent Lieutenant James Cook to Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus of 3 June 1769, part of an international effort to measure the distance to the Sun, with secret orders to search for a southern continent. With the help of the Ra'iatean navigator Tupaia, Cook circumnavigated and mapped both main islands of New Zealand and then charted the east coast of Australia, landing at Botany Bay in April 1770. The naturalists Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander collected thousands of specimens. Cook's three voyages transformed European knowledge of the Pacific and prepared the way for British colonisation of Australia and New Zealand, with profound consequences for Indigenous peoples; he was killed in Hawaii in 1779.

title: Great Bengal famine of 1770
summary: After the 1769 monsoon failed, famine and disease killed millions in Bengal and Bihar while East India Company revenue demands were kept up.
description: In 1765 the East India Company had gained the diwani, the right to collect revenue, in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, while civil administration stayed with the nawab's officials. After poor harvests in 1768 and the failure of the monsoon rains in 1769, famine spread across the lower Ganges plain in 1769–70, accompanied by smallpox. Land revenue continued to be collected, and was even raised in some areas, the Company bought rice for its troops, and Company servants and merchants were accused of monopolising grain, while relief was minimal. Company officials at the time reported that about a third of the population, often put at 10 million people, had died, but some modern historians consider this inflated and estimate at least 1–2 million deaths. The disaster hastened the end of the dual system, with the Company taking over direct administration in 1772, and fed criticism in Britain that contributed to the Regulating Act of 1773.

title: Tartaria and the 'mud flood' conspiracy theory
summary: An internet conspiracy theory claims a vast advanced empire called Tartaria was erased from history, its cities buried by a global 'mud flood'.
description: The theory grew out of Russian nationalist pseudohistory, including Anatoly Fomenko's 'New Chronology', and spread on websites and social media from the 2010s. It builds on the name 'Tartary' or 'Grand Tartary', which European maps and reference works of the 16th to 18th centuries, including the first edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica (1771), used for the little-known lands of northern and central Asia. Proponents claim this was a technologically advanced worldwide civilisation whose grand architecture, including 19th-century public buildings and world's fair pavilions, was later misattributed, and that a cataclysmic 'mud flood' buried its cities, explaining partly sunken ground floors and basement windows.
mainstreamView: 'Tartary' was a vague European name for the inner Asian lands of peoples such as the Mongols, Manchus and Turkic groups, never a single state, let alone a global one. The buildings cited are well documented by architects' plans, construction records, newspapers and photographs, and below-grade ground floors result from cities raising street levels, gradual soil build-up and deliberate basement design. No archaeological or geological evidence shows a worldwide mud layer in the 18th or 19th centuries, and the theory relies on misread maps, decontextualised images and coincidences.

title: Partitions of Poland
summary: Russia, Prussia and Austria carved up the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in three partitions, erasing it from the map for 123 years.
description: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, once one of Europe's largest states, had been weakened by an elective monarchy, the liberum veto and foreign interference. In 1772 its three neighbours annexed about a third of its territory. Reform efforts, notably the Constitution of 3 May 1791, one of the first modern written national constitutions, provoked a Russian invasion and a second partition in 1793. After the failed Kościuszko Uprising of 1794, the remaining lands were divided in 1795. Poland did not regain independence until 1918.

title: Watt's steam engine
summary: James Watt's separate condenser made steam engines far more fuel-efficient, and with Matthew Boulton he built engines to power mines, mills and factories.
description: While repairing a model Newcomen engine at the University of Glasgow in the 1760s, Watt realised that much fuel was wasted by repeatedly heating and cooling the cylinder, and devised a separate condenser, patented in 1769. In partnership with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton, whose Soho works became their base, the first commercial engines were installed in 1776, helped by John Wilkinson's precise cylinder boring. Watt's engines used roughly a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine. In the 1780s he added rotary motion, double action and the centrifugal governor, allowing steam to drive factory machinery and freeing industry from dependence on water power. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

title: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations
summary: Adam Smith argued that the division of labour, the extent of the market and competition, rather than mercantilist restrictions, drive national prosperity.
description: Smith, a former professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow and a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, wrote much of An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations in his home town of Kirkcaldy. Opening with the example of a pin factory, he argued that the division of labour and the extent of the market determine productivity, and attacked the mercantile system of tariffs, monopolies and colonial trade restrictions. He also warned of collusion among merchants and supported public education and certain public works. Published in London, the book became the founding text of classical economics.

title: US Declaration of Independence
summary: Thirteen British colonies in North America declared independence, asserting that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.
description: Fighting between colonial militias and British troops had begun at Lexington and Concord in April 1775. Meeting in Philadelphia, the Second Continental Congress voted for independence on 2 July 1776 and adopted the Declaration, drafted chiefly by Thomas Jefferson, on 4 July. Its preamble, drawing on Enlightenment ideas, asserted unalienable rights to 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness', although slavery remained legal in every colony. With French support from 1778, the Americans won the Revolutionary War, and Britain recognised the United States in the Treaty of Paris of 1783. The Declaration inspired later revolutionaries and rights movements around the world.

title: Rebellion of Túpac Amaru II
summary: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, an Indigenous noble claiming Inca descent as Túpac Amaru II, led a massive Andean uprising against Spanish colonial abuses.
description: Protesting forced labour, the reparto system of compulsory purchases and new taxes imposed under the Bourbon reforms, Túpac Amaru II seized and executed the local corregidor Antonio de Arriaga near Tinta in November 1780. The uprising spread across southern Peru and Upper Peru, where Túpac Katari besieged La Paz in 1781. Túpac Amaru was captured and executed in Cusco's main square in May 1781, but fighting continued until 1783, and perhaps 100,000 people died. Spanish authorities responded by suppressing Inca symbols and institutions, and the rebellion later became an emblem for independence and Indigenous movements.

title: Laki fissure eruption
summary: An eight-month fissure eruption in Iceland released vast amounts of sulphur, killing about a fifth of Iceland's people and spreading a toxic haze over Europe.
description: The Laki (Lakagígar) fissure, a 27 km row of craters, erupted about 14 cubic kilometres of basalt lava and some 120 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide. Fluorine poisoning and the loss of grazing killed most of Iceland's livestock, and the resulting famine, the 'Mist Hardships', killed about 20–25 percent of the population. A sulphurous haze spread across Europe in the summer of 1783, coinciding with excess deaths in England and France, and the following winter was unusually severe in Europe and North America. It was one of the largest eruptions in historical times and is studied as an analogue for the hazards of large fissure eruptions.

title: United States Constitution
summary: Delegates at Philadelphia drafted a federal constitution with separated powers and checks and balances, the oldest codified national constitution in force.
description: The Articles of Confederation had left the national government unable to tax or regulate trade, and a convention met in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise them. Instead the delegates, presided over by George Washington and strongly shaped by James Madison, drafted a new framework dividing power between the states and a federal government of legislative, executive and judicial branches. Compromises gave small states equal representation in the Senate and counted three-fifths of enslaved people when apportioning seats in the House. After ratification debates, including the essays of The Federalist, it took effect in 1789, and the Bill of Rights was added in 1791.

title: James Hutton and the discovery of deep time
summary: At Siccar Point, James Hutton saw tilted rock layers capped by younger ones, evidence that Earth's history spans immensely long ages.
description: The Edinburgh naturalist James Hutton presented his Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785, arguing that rocks are formed, eroded and uplifted by slow processes still observable today, operating in repeated cycles. In 1788 he showed his friends John Playfair and James Hall the unconformity at Siccar Point, where nearly vertical greywacke strata are overlain by gently dipping red sandstone, and Playfair later wrote that 'the mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time'. Hutton concluded that the Earth showed 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end'. His ideas, popularised by Playfair and later Charles Lyell, laid the foundations of modern geology and of the long timescales on which this timeline rests.

title: First Fleet founds a penal colony at Sydney
summary: Eleven British ships carrying about 1,400 people, most of them convicts and marines, established the colony of New South Wales at Sydney Cove.
description: After losing its American colonies, Britain needed a new destination for transported convicts, and Cook's visit of 1770 had identified Botany Bay. Commanded by Captain Arthur Phillip, the First Fleet arrived there in January 1788 but moved to the better harbour of Port Jackson, raising the flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January. The settlement struggled with near-famine in its first years. Colonisation dispossessed the Aboriginal peoples who had lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, and a smallpox epidemic in 1789 killed many of the Eora people around Sydney. The date is now Australia Day, a public holiday that many Indigenous Australians mark as Invasion Day or Survival Day.

title: Lavoisier's chemical revolution
summary: Lavoisier, who named oxygen and hydrogen and overthrew phlogiston theory, listed the elements and stated conservation of mass in his 1789 Elementary Treatise.
description: Oxygen had been isolated by Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Joseph Priestley, but through careful weighing in closed vessels Lavoisier showed in the 1770s and 1780s that combustion and respiration involve combination with this component of air, which he named oxygen, overturning the phlogiston theory. With colleagues he devised a systematic chemical nomenclature in 1787, and his Traité élémentaire de chimie of 1789 listed 33 'simple substances' and stated that mass is conserved in chemical reactions. His wife and collaborator Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier translated scientific texts and illustrated his apparatus. A former tax farmer, he was guillotined during the Terror in 1794.

title: The French Revolution
summary: A fiscal crisis became a revolution that abolished France's absolute monarchy and feudal privileges, proclaimed the Rights of Man and founded a republic.
description: Facing bankruptcy, Louis XVI summoned the Estates-General in May 1789; its Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, and Parisian crowds stormed the Bastille on 14 July. The Assembly abolished feudal privileges and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. War with European monarchies from 1792, the overthrow of the monarchy and the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793 were followed by the Terror, in which some 17,000 people were officially executed. The revolutionary decade ended with Napoleon Bonaparte's coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799. Its ideas of popular sovereignty, citizenship and legal equality shaped modern politics worldwide.

title: The Haitian Revolution
summary: Enslaved people in French Saint-Domingue rose in revolt, abolished slavery and founded Haiti, the first state created by a successful slave uprising.
description: Saint-Domingue was the richest colony in the Caribbean, producing much of the world's sugar and coffee with the labour of about half a million enslaved Africans. A massive uprising began in the Northern Plain in August 1791, and amid war with Britain and Spain the French commissioners abolished slavery in 1793, confirmed by Paris in 1794. Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved general, came to govern the colony, but Napoleon sent an expedition in 1802 to restore French control, and Toussaint died in a French prison. Under Jean-Jacques Dessalines the revolutionary armies, aided by yellow fever among French troops, defeated the French and declared Haiti independent on 1 January 1804. The revolution alarmed slaveholding societies across the Atlantic world and inspired the enslaved and abolitionists.

title: Kamehameha I unifies Hawaii
summary: Using Western ships and firearms, Kamehameha of Hawaiʻi Island conquered Maui and Oʻahu, winning the decisive Battle of Nuʻuanu.
description: Kamehameha, a chief from the island of Hawaiʻi, rose to power in the wars that followed the death of his uncle Kalaniʻōpuʻu in 1782, using European and American weapons, ships and advisers acquired through the growing Pacific trade. In 1795 he invaded Oʻahu and defeated Kalanikūpule at Nuʻuanu, where many defenders were driven over the steep cliffs of the Pali. Kauaʻi and Niʻihau accepted his rule peacefully in 1810, completing the unification of the Kingdom of Hawaii. The kingdom he founded lasted until its overthrow by American-backed businessmen in 1893.

title: Jenner's smallpox vaccine
summary: Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox and showed that it protected him against smallpox, creating the first vaccine.
description: Smallpox killed an estimated 400,000 Europeans a year in the late 18th century. Variolation, deliberate infection with material from smallpox sores, had long been practised in Asia and Africa and was popularised in Britain in the 1720s, but it carried real risks. Jenner, a country doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, tested the folk belief that milkmaids who caught cowpox were immune: he inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with cowpox and later exposed him to smallpox, which did not take. His 1798 publication launched vaccination, named from the Latin vacca, 'cow', which spread worldwide within a few years and led eventually to the eradication of smallpox, declared by the World Health Organization in 1980.

title: Illuminati conspiracy theory
summary: Writers claimed the Bavarian Illuminati, a secret society banned in 1785, survived to cause the French Revolution, a myth still told of a hidden world elite.
description: The Order of the Illuminati was founded at Ingolstadt in Bavaria on 1 May 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, a professor of canon law, as a secret society opposed to superstition, clerical influence over public life and abuses of state power. It recruited largely through Masonic lodges and probably never had more than a couple of thousand members, and Bavarian edicts against secret societies in 1784 and 1785 broke it up. In 1797–98 the French Jesuit Augustin Barruel, in his Memoirs Illustrating the History of Jacobinism, and the Scottish scientist John Robison, in Proofs of a Conspiracy, claimed that surviving Illuminati and Freemasons had plotted and caused the French Revolution. Their books inspired an 'Illuminati scare' in the United States in 1798, later fed antisemitic conspiracy theories, and underlie modern claims that the Illuminati are a hidden elite controlling governments, finance and entertainment.
mainstreamView: Historians agree that the Bavarian Illuminati were a small, short-lived society that had effectively collapsed by 1785, years before the French Revolution, and there is no evidence that it survived or directed any later events. The Revolution is explained by well-documented causes, including the monarchy's fiscal crisis, social and political tensions, poor harvests and Enlightenment ideas, while Barruel and Robison relied on suspicion and guilt by association rather than evidence. Modern Illuminati claims are unfalsifiable conspiracy theories with no documentary support.
